extracted.intended_audience: legal academics, patent scholars, patent office policymakers, and patent practitioners (litigators/examiners)
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical analysis of how U.S. patent examiners use prior art submitted by applicants (versus art they locate themselves) during prosecution and how that affects patent quality, litigation presumptions, and related policy debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor / applicant disclosure obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applicants must disclose any material prior inventions, uses, and publications ('prior art') of which they are aware to the PTO; failure to do so can render the resulting patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty of candor applies throughout prosecution; applicants are obliged to disclose any new material art they learn of even after applications are submitted. Deliberate failure to disclose material prior art is inequitable conduct that renders the entire patent unenforceable. The doctrine may still apply to non-prior-art information (e.g., false assertions of unexpected results).

rubrics_metrics.name: No absolute obligation on applicants to search for prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must disclose material prior art they are aware of, but have no obligation to conduct an independent search for prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although applicants are close to the invention and may be best positioned to know about relevant prior art, the law does not require applicants to search proactively; incentives (presumption of validity, inequitable conduct) influence disclosure/search behavior and vary by industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity (standard of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Issued patents enjoy a strong presumption of validity that can be overcome only by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is grounded on the idea that the PTO has vetted the patent. Courts have questioned extending the presumption to art not before the PTO; prior case law (Ultra-Tex, KSR, Microsoft v. i4i) affects how prior art not considered by the examiner is treated and jury instructions may reflect that it's easier to prove invalidity using evidence not considered by the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether prior art was before the examiner matters to weight of invalidity evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether prior art was actually before the examiner affects the likelihood that factfinders will invalidate an issued patent on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work shows factfinders are far more likely to invalidate a patent based on prior art not before the PTO; judges and juries may defer to an examiner's expertise when the examiner considered the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101: Subject Matter Eligibility / Utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. §101 when the claimed invention is directed to ineligible subject matter (e.g., law of nature, physical phenomena, abstract idea) or is not useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rejections are not based on prior art and are more common in computers and biotechnology art units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102 if the claimed subject matter is not novel (described in a printed publication or publicly used or sold in the U.S. more than one year before filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102 rejections rely on prior art and are a primary focus when assessing whether applicant-submitted references are used by examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 103: Non-Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 when the claimed invention is an obvious advance over what was known at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like 102, 103 rejections depend on prior art; the paper analyzes who supplied the references used in these rejections (applicant vs examiner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 112: Disclosure (written description & enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. §112 for failing to adequately describe and enable the invention or for failing to clearly define what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 112 rejections are more common in biotechnology and are not prior-art-based rejections; therefore not the core focus of prior-art usage analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 121: Restriction requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may be subject to restriction requirements under §121 when it includes two or more independent and distinct inventions; the PTO requires restriction to a single invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restriction requirements are not rejections on the merits and are not considered further in analyses of prior-art-based rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-of-citation as an evaluative dimension (applicant vs examiner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a prior art reference was submitted by an applicant (IDS) or located/cited by an examiner is a key determinant of whether the reference is used in an examiner's rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: applicants submitted ~73–76% of references overall, but only ~12.7% of references used in examiner rejections come from applicants; only ~2% of applicant references are used in rejections vs ~36% of examiner references. The source effect persists after controlling for patent class, type of art, continuation/divisional status, and application year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of prior art as an evaluative dimension (U.S. patents, foreign patents, non-patent literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of prior art are unequally likely to be used in rejections; examiners disproportionately rely on U.S. patents they locate themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most non-patent literature and foreign patent citations are submitted by applicants, and examiners use a much higher share of examiner-supplied U.S. patent citations (e.g., >90% of U.S. patents used in rejections originate from examiner searches). Non-patent and foreign art are less likely to be used overall, but examiner-found foreign patents may be more likely to be used than examiner-found U.S. patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of applicant submissions (original vs late/post-docket pre-first office action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether applicant-submitted references arrive with the original filing or later (post-docket but before first office action) could affect their likelihood of being used by examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical result: ~20% of applicant citations to U.S. and foreign patents arrive post-docket but pre-first office action; later-arriving applicant art is not substantially more likely to be used in rejections, which weakens the hypothesis that applicants simply 'drafted around' original-disclosed art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance/quality of applicant-submitted art (including foreign search/X & Y EPO citations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality or relevance of applicant-submitted art (e.g., citations flagged as X or Y on EPO search reports) may influence whether U.S. examiners use that art in rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late-arriving EPO-listed (X/Y) citations have a modestly higher likelihood (~10 percentage points in pooled sample) of being used than other late applicant cites, but even EPO-listed U.S. patents are substantially less likely (~26 percentage points) to be used than examiner-found citations, suggesting relevance does not fully explain the examiner preference for their own finds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flooding the PTO (excessive citation lists) as an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting very large numbers of references (IDSs with 'box loads' of references) might render applicant submissions less useful, potentially overwhelming examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews and anecdotal evidence suggest examiners dislike excessive, low-relevance citations. Empirical interaction tests (applicant citation * total citations quartile) show only a small and statistically insignificant decrease in probability that a given applicant citation is used as the volume increases, so flooding is unlikely to be the primary explanation for low use rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner workload/time constraints affecting examination quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners have substantial caseloads and limited time (reported average ~18 hours over 3–5 years per application) to search for, evaluate, and apply prior art, which may affect how they use submitted references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resource constraints and skewed incentives at the PTO have been cited as reasons for problems with patent quality and the practical operation of presumptions of validity; they plausibly contribute to examiner focus on references they find themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/statistical controls and evaluation dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating citation-use patterns empirically, one should control for patent-class (three-digit), whether the citing patent is a continuation or divisional, application year, and type/source/timing of citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper uses linear probability models (and logit analogues) with class and year fixed effects, interactions between source and type of art, and clustering of robust standard errors on citing patents to isolate the effect of applicant vs examiner source on probability of use in rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy implication criterion: whether bringing more prior art before examiners will improve patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A key evaluative question is whether policies that encourage more or earlier submission of prior art (by applicants, third-party searchers, or via worksharing with foreign offices) will reduce issuance of weak patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examiners overwhelmingly rely on art they find themselves, proposals to increase applicant or third-party submissions may generate prior art that is not considered and therefore may have limited effect on patent quality; this has implications for reforms aimed at 'bringing more prior art' to the PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct doctrine's practical effect as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether failure to disclose prior art (inequitable conduct) remains a major problem depends in part on whether applicant-submitted art is actually used by examiners during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiners rarely use applicant-submitted art in rejections, then the practical harms of nondisclosure (as commonly conceived) may be smaller, although inequitable conduct can still matter for other types of misrepresentations.
